extracted.intended_audience: index equity asset managers, institutional investors (BlackRock clients), corporate boards and governance professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Global principles that guide BlackRock Investment Stewardship’s engagement and proxy voting on behalf of index equity clients, focusing on financial materiality and long-term financial interests. The document explains expectations of company governance, disclosures, voting execution, conflicts management, and sustainability-related oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stewardship purpose and fiduciary duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Investment stewardship serves as a link between clients and the companies they invest in and is one of the ways BlackRock fulfills its fiduciary responsibilities as an asset manager on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS takes a long-term approach and a financial materiality-based approach focused solely on advancing clients’ long-term financial interests; stewardship includes engagement, voting, contributing to industry dialogue, and reporting to clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement to inform voting
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS engages with boards and management to deepen understanding of a company's business model and how they oversee material business risks and opportunities over time to inform voting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engagement topics reflect matters that, in BIS' experience, impact long-term financial returns; engagement is not used to change or influence control of a company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proxy voting consistent with client objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: As a fiduciary, BlackRock must make proxy voting determinations consistent with the investment objectives of clients who have delegated voting authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vote decisions reflect BIS’ reasonable and independent judgment of what is in clients’ long-term financial interests and are informed by company disclosures, peer comparisons, third-party research, and engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: General presumption to support management
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, BIS supports the vote recommendations of the board and management at companies with sound corporate governance and strong financial returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When concerns exist, BIS may convey them through withholding support for director elections or management’s recommendation on shareholder proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareholder rights expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Shareholders should generally have rights to vote to elect/remove/nominate directors, approve auditors, amend charter/bylaws, vote on key board decisions, and access sufficient and timely information on material governance, strategic, and business matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rights are underpinned by corporate laws, regulations, and listing rules in most markets; BIS considers access to timely material information essential for informed voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality- and market-aware application of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS Global Principles are not prescriptive but applied pragmatically, taking into account company-specific factors including sector, market, and business environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a regional level, companies should at minimum observe accepted domestic corporate governance standards or explain how their approach better supports durable long-term value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on board effectiveness and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Stewardship efforts focus on the effectiveness of the board of directors in setting, executing, and overseeing strategy consistent with long-term financial interests of investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS assesses board governance frameworks, clarity of board and committee roles, and disclosure of material risks and how management identifies and mitigates them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board disclosure on strategy and risk oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards should provide clear descriptions of their role, the committees, how directors engage with and oversee management, and disclosure of material risks affecting long-term strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where strategic targets are missed or restated, helpful disclosure includes explanation of changes and the board’s role in reviewing revised targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for withholding director elections when oversight inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS may consider not supporting the election of directors who have particular responsibility for corporate governance and risk oversight when the company has not adequately disclosed or demonstrated board fulfillment of these responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voting on director elections is a tool to signal concerns about board oversight and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular accountability through director elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors should stand for election on a regular basis, ideally annually, to ensure timely shareholder accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not annual, boards should have a rotation policy ensuring all directors are reconfirmed over a board cycle, with a proportion of directors up for election each meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board quality, refreshment and tenure balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards should periodically bring new directors to refresh thinking, while maintaining continuity and succession planning; BIS considers overall average tenure and seeks balance between experience and fresh perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should regularly review how nominees contribute to board effectiveness considering independence, time commitments, breadth and relevance of experience and skillsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director independence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Director independence from management, significant shareholders, or related parties is central; BIS generally considers it good practice for independent directors to make up a board majority (or at least one-third in controlled companies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common impediments include recent employment, representing a substantial shareholder, interlocking directorates, or any relationship that could materially interfere with acting in the company's best interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior independent board leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards are most effective with a senior, independent board leader, either an independent chair or a lead independent director where the chair is not independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role includes shaping agenda, ensuring adequate information, encouraging independent participation, and being available to meet shareholders where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent-majority committees for conflicted matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective oversight of conflicts or matters requiring additional focus is best achieved with board committees composed of a majority of independent directors (subject to market norms and ownership structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common specialized committees include audit, nominations, and compensation; ad hoc committees should be formed for special transactions or to investigate significant adverse events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient director capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors must commit appropriate time to board and committee matters and not take on excessive roles that would impair their ability to fulfill duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity should allow directors to meet responsibilities including during unforeseen events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition disclosure and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: When nominating directors, companies should provide sufficient information for shareholders to assess each nominee’s capabilities, suitability, and fit within overall board composition and strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures should explain how collective experience and individual skillsets align with long-term strategy and may address diversity considerations, including gender goals where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit committee oversight and auditor independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Audit committees (or equivalent) are responsible for overseeing the independent auditor and internal audit, financial reporting, and internal control frameworks; auditors should be independent and free of impediments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations include clear committee charters, demonstrated relevant expertise of committee members, rotation plans, disclosure/explanation of non-audit fees, annual procedures to assess auditor independence and audit quality, and timely disclosure of remediation for key/critical audit matters or restatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk oversight via audit or risk committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Audit or risk committees should periodically review the company’s risk assessment and management policies, significant risks and exposures, and management’s steps to address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of detailed disclosures, BIS may conclude a company is not adequately managing risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital structure and pre-emptive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital structure critically impacts shareholder value and priority; pre-emptive rights protect against dilution and are a key protection for shareholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS is concerned with share classes that have equivalent economic exposure but differentiated voting rights and generally supports 'one share, one vote' bylaws for registered shareholders, while recognizing some markets' transitional uses of dual-class structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of dual-class share structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where dual-class shares exist, companies should review structures regularly and seek periodic shareholder approval, giving unaffiliated shareholders opportunity to affirm or establish mechanisms to end/phase out controlling structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should minimize costs to shareholders and provide mechanisms to end controlling structures at an appropriate time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mergers, acquisitions and special situations evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS’ primary consideration in transactions is the long-term financial interests of clients as shareholders; BIS reviews whether transactions have unanimous board support, were negotiated at arm’s length, and whether economic and strategic rationale is clearly explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS may seek reassurance that executives/board members’ interests did not adversely affect shareholders; related-party transactions should be recommended by independent directors, ideally with independent appraisal and separate votes of non-conflicted parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to mechanisms limiting share disposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Shareholder rights should allow disposal of company shares in the open market without unnecessary restriction; mechanisms that limit sale rights are contrary to property rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareholder rights plans should be subject to shareholder approval upon introduction and periodically thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive compensation linkage to long-term performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive compensation should support long-term financial value creation through a clear link between variable pay and operational/financial performance, aligning executives and shareholders through equity ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate ambitious targets aligned with strategy; long-term incentive plans should be distinct from annual compensation and encourage multi-year performance; sustainability criteria may be included but must be set as rigorously as financial targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation committee practices and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards and compensation committees should consider company-specific circumstances, risk profile, and retention needs; guard against contractual arrangements that pay material compensation for early termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary adjustments should be disclosed with rationale; peer group benchmarking is useful but companies should explain how outcomes reward performance rather than only benchmarking-driven increases. Clawback provisions are considered good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on one-off bonuses and reasonableness of pensions
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS is not supportive of one-off or special bonuses unrelated to company or individual performance; pension contributions and deferred compensation should be reasonable in light of market practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where discretion is used or unusual arrangements exist, expect disclosure and alignment with shareholder interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for misaligned compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where compensation is misaligned with company performance, BIS may not support management’s compensation proposals and may withhold support for members of compensation committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vote decisions on compensation are based on disclosed rigor relative to strategy, circumstances, and market developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate form changes and shareholder approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards proposing changes to corporate form (e.g., conversion to public benefit corporation) should put the change to a shareholder vote if not already required by law and provide documentation explaining shareholder and stakeholder impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS generally supports management proposals if shareholders’ financial interests are adequately protected; evaluations are case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case treatment of shareholder proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS votes on shareholder proposals by assessing implications for long-term financial value creation, materiality of the request, and whether disclosures requested are additive to investor understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess consistency between formal request, supporting documentation and proponents’ communications; consider costs/benefits, company practices relative to peers, legal effect (advisory vs binding), and avoid support for micromanaging or proposals inconsistent with long-term value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of proponents and proposal packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: It is helpful when companies disclose the names of proponents or advisors for shareholder proposals; proposals may bundle topics or include supporting statements on unrelated matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When BIS supports a proposal, it is not necessarily endorsing every element of the proponent’s reasoning; votes are on the proposal as phrased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust disclosure on material sustainability-related risks and opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should provide robust disclosure enabling investors to evaluate strategy and business practices related to material sustainability-related risks and opportunities and demonstrate integration into strategy, risk management, metrics and targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardized disclosure frameworks (e.g., ISSB S1/S2) are useful though not mandated; companies should highlight industry- or company-specific metrics and may phase reporting over several years; industry initiatives and assurance processes are helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate-related disclosures and transition planning
rubrics_metrics.description: For companies facing material climate risks, BIS finds it helpful when companies disclose how they intend to deliver long-term financial performance through the low-carbon transition, including transition plans where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek understanding of strategies across climate scenarios, short/medium/long-term targets (ideally science-based where available) for scope 1 and 2 emissions; treat scope 3 disclosures as different due to complexity but welcome good-faith disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-related risks and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: For companies materially reliant on natural capital, disclosures on nature-related dependencies and impacts help assess board oversight of these risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TNFD recommendations may be useful but are not voting items; recognize different reporting standards may apply by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and oversight of workforce, supply chains and communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should identify key stakeholders material to business and disclose how they consider stakeholder interests in decision-making, particularly workforce issues important to long-term value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful disclosures include identification of stakeholders, workforce skills planning, board oversight, monitoring/due-diligence to identify adverse impacts, and grievance/remediation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: BIS governance and oversight of stewardship activities
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS maintains a governance structure including a BIS Global Oversight Committee chaired by Global Heads of Investment Stewardship and regional heads overseeing activities in the Americas, APAC, and EMEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee reviews and approves amendments to Global Principles and regional guidelines, reviews votes cast, material process issues, procedural changes, and risk oversight considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vote execution principles and logistical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS has processes to consider all proxies where authorized and will submit voting decisions or refrain from voting when logistical issues arise; votes reflect independent judgment without regard to relationships with issuers or affiliates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistical issues include untimely notice, restrictions on foreigners, in-person voting requirements, share-blocking, translation difficulties, regulatory constraints, and powers of attorney requirements; BIS votes on a 'best-efforts' basis and may not vote if costs outweigh client benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts management and independence of stewardship function
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS is separate from BlackRock’s sales, business partnership or vendor management activities; BlackRock maintains policies and procedures designed to prevent undue influence on BIS’ proxy voting activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts procedures cover relationships between investee companies and BlackRock, its funds, affiliates, or employees; see BIS disclosures for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securities lending and recall decisions for voting
rubrics_metrics.description: BlackRock acts as securities lending agent when authorized; lent securities cannot be voted unless recalled, and BlackRock may recall securities to vote based on fiduciary evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions to recall weigh potential securities lending revenue versus potential long-term financial value of voting; typically BIS anticipates voting value is less than lending revenue but may recall in limited cases; procedures are periodically reviewed and recall feasibility affected by record date timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting Choice program and client-directed voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting Choice provides eligible clients the opportunity to participate in proxy voting where legally and operationally viable, enabling eligible clients to have shares voted according to their selected policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available for eligible institutional pooled funds, SMAs, and certain retail accounts in specified markets; shares attributed to BlackRock portfolios may be voted differently depending on client authorizations; client selections are not disclosed without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and vote transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS is committed to transparency and provides clients with information on engagement and voting policies and activities through regional voting guidelines, commentaries, and quarterly reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BlackRock publishes regional voting guidelines and makes disclosures on its website and through direct client communications to inform clients and companies.
